_note: Plain-language, educational descriptions. Not medical advice; shapes come from an automatic computer segmentation and can be wrong.

frontal.name: Frontal lobe
frontal.description: The front part of the brain. It helps with planning, decision-making, attention, controlling behaviour, speech production (usually on the left) and starting voluntary movements.

parietal.name: Parietal lobe
parietal.description: Sits behind the frontal lobe at the top of the head. It brings together touch, body position and vision so you know where things (and your own body) are in space.

temporal.name: Temporal lobe
temporal.description: Lies on the side of the brain near the ears. It handles hearing, understanding language (usually on the left), recognising faces and objects, and helps form memories.

occipital.name: Occipital lobe
occipital.description: The back of the brain. It is the main centre for vision: it turns signals from the eyes into shapes, colours and motion.

cingulate.name: Cingulate cortex
cingulate.description: A band of cortex on the inner surface of each hemisphere, wrapped around the deep fibre bridge between the two halves. It is involved in emotion, motivation, attention and noticing mistakes.

insula.name: Insula
insula.description: A region of cortex folded deep inside the side of the brain. It senses the body's inner state (heartbeat, hunger, temperature) and contributes to taste, emotion and self-awareness.

cerebral_wm.name: Cerebral white matter
cerebral_wm.description: Bundles of insulated nerve fibres that connect different parts of the brain, like the brain's wiring. The insulation (myelin) is fatty, which is why it looks bright on a T1 scan.

thalamus.name: Thalamus
thalamus.description: A walnut-sized relay station in the middle of the brain. Almost all sensory information (except smell) passes through it on the way to the cortex; it also helps regulate sleep and alertness.

caudate.name: Caudate nucleus
caudate.description: A C-shaped structure next to the fluid-filled ventricles. Part of the basal ganglia, it helps with learning habits, planning movements and goal-directed behaviour.

putamen.name: Putamen
putamen.description: A rounded structure deep in each hemisphere and part of the basal ganglia. It helps control and smooth out movements and supports learning of skills and routines.

pallidum.name: Globus pallidus
pallidum.description: Sits just inside the putamen. Part of the basal ganglia, it works like a brake and accelerator for movement signals, helping keep movements smooth.

accumbens.name: Nucleus accumbens
accumbens.description: A small area where the caudate and putamen meet. It is part of the brain's reward system and is involved in motivation and pleasure.

hippocampus.name: Hippocampus
hippocampus.description: A curved, seahorse-shaped structure inside the temporal lobe. It is key for forming new memories and for finding your way around.

amygdala.name: Amygdala
amygdala.description: An almond-shaped cluster just in front of the hippocampus. It helps process emotions, especially fear, and tags memories with emotional importance.

ventral_dc.name: Ventral diencephalon
ventral_dc.description: A group of small structures under the thalamus, including the hypothalamus, which helps control body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep and hormones.

lateral_ventricle.name: Lateral ventricle
lateral_ventricle.description: A C-shaped, fluid-filled space in each hemisphere. The ventricles make and hold cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which cushions the brain. Their size varies a lot between healthy people.

third_ventricle.name: Third ventricle
third_ventricle.description: A narrow, fluid-filled slit in the midline between the left and right thalamus. It connects the lateral ventricles to the fourth ventricle.

fourth_ventricle.name: Fourth ventricle
fourth_ventricle.description: A small fluid-filled space between the brainstem and the cerebellum. Fluid flows from here into the space around the brain and spinal cord.

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.description: Connects the brain to the spinal cord. It runs automatic functions such as breathing, heart rate, swallowing and sleep cycles, and carries signals between brain and body.

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.description: The 'little brain' at the back, under the cerebrum. It fine-tunes movement, balance and posture, and helps with timing and learning motor skills.

vertebra_c1.name: C1 vertebra (atlas)
vertebra_c1.description: The top bone of the spine, a ring with no body that carries the skull. Nodding “yes” happens mostly at the joint between the skull and the atlas.

vertebra_c2.name: C2 vertebra (axis)
vertebra_c2.description: The second neck bone. A peg (the dens) sticks up from it into the ring of the atlas, and the atlas turns around it: most of shaking your head “no” happens here.

vertebra_c3.name: C3 vertebra
vertebra_c3.description: One of the seven neck bones (cervical vertebrae). Each has a solid body at the front and a bony ring at the back that shields the spinal cord.

vertebra_c4.name: C4 vertebra
vertebra_c4.description: A middle neck bone. Nerves leaving the spine at about this height help control the diaphragm, the main breathing muscle.

vertebra_c5.name: C5 vertebra
vertebra_c5.description: A lower-middle neck bone. Nerves at this height help move the shoulder and bend the elbow.

vertebra_c6.name: C6 vertebra
vertebra_c6.description: A lower neck bone. The neck bends a lot around C5 and C6, so these levels often show wear-and-tear changes, also in people without any symptoms.

vertebra_c7.name: C7 vertebra
vertebra_c7.description: The lowest neck bone. Its long spine is the bump you can feel at the base of the back of the neck.

vertebra_t1.name: T1 vertebra
vertebra_t1.description: The first chest (thoracic) vertebra, where the first pair of ribs attaches. It marks where the neck ends.

intervertebral_discs.name: Intervertebral discs
intervertebral_discs.description: Soft cushions between the vertebrae, with a tough outer ring and a gel-like centre. They absorb shocks and let the neck bend and turn. Discs naturally lose some water with age.

spinal_cord.name: Spinal cord
spinal_cord.description: The bundle of nerves that carries signals between the brain and the body. It continues from the brainstem down inside the bony canal of the vertebrae, bathed in fluid (CSF).

caudalanteriorcingulate: Part of the cingulate cortex involved in attention, motivation and monitoring actions.
caudalmiddlefrontal: Helps plan movements and control where you look and what you pay attention to.
cuneus: A wedge of visual cortex on the inner surface at the back, processing basic visual information.
entorhinal: A gateway between the hippocampus and the rest of the cortex, important for memory and navigation.
fusiform: On the underside of the temporal lobe; helps recognise faces, words and objects.
inferiorparietal: Combines sight, sound and touch; involved in attention, language and understanding space.
inferiortemporal: Helps recognise objects and shapes you see.
isthmuscingulate: A narrow part of the cingulate linking it to memory areas; involved in memory and orientation.
lateraloccipital: Outer visual cortex that helps recognise objects and shapes.
lateralorbitofrontal: Above the eye sockets; helps weigh rewards and adjust behaviour.
lingual: Visual cortex on the underside at the back; involved in vision, including reading and colour.
medialorbitofrontal: Above the eyes near the midline; involved in valuing choices and emotions.
middletemporal: Involved in understanding language, word meaning and seeing motion.
parahippocampal: Next to the hippocampus; helps remember places and scenes.
paracentral: On the inner surface at the top; controls movement and feeling in the legs and feet.
parsopercularis: Part of the inferior frontal gyrus; on the left side usually involved in speech production.
parsorbitalis: Front-most part of the inferior frontal gyrus; involved in language meaning.
parstriangularis: Part of the inferior frontal gyrus; on the left side usually involved in language.
pericalcarine: The primary visual cortex, the first stop in the cortex for signals from the eyes.
postcentral: The primary touch area: it receives feelings of touch, temperature and body position.
posteriorcingulate: Involved in memory, attention and mind-wandering; a hub of the brain's resting network.
precentral: The primary motor area: it sends the commands that move your muscles.
precuneus: On the inner surface of the parietal lobe; involved in imagery, memory and self-reflection.
rostralanteriorcingulate: Front part of the cingulate; involved in emotion and mood regulation.
rostralmiddlefrontal: Involved in working memory, planning and complex thinking.
superiorfrontal: The top of the frontal lobe; involved in self-awareness, working memory and planning movements.
superiorparietal: Helps guide reaching and grasping and keeps track of where your body is.
superiortemporal: Contains hearing areas; on the left side usually helps understand speech.
supramarginal: Involved in touch perception, language and understanding others' actions.
transversetemporal: The primary hearing area (Heschl's gyrus), the first stop in the cortex for sound.
insula: Folded deep inside; senses the body's inner state and contributes to taste and emotion.
